source.title: SURGE: On the Potential of Large Language Models as General-Purpose Surrogate Code Executors
source.authors: Bohan Lyu; Siqiao Huang; Zichen Liang

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures surrogate-execution task performance across model sizes and training steps, rather than measuring held-out pretraining cross-entropy or fitting the original scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a scaling experiment on the formal-language subset and benchmark comparisons relevant to downstream task performance (V6). Other benchmark results that do not compare scale or bear on a claim version are not cataloged here.
record.test_reason: The paper reports downstream task performance across model sizes in a new setting: LLMs predicting code execution results. It does this two ways: a fine-tuning sweep of Qwen 0.5B–7B on the FL subset (Fig. 2) and benchmark scores for Qwen-2.5 and Qwen-2.5-Coder families at 0.5B–72B (Table 5). Both bear on V6. No pretraining loss, fitted laws or allocation are measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say fine-tuning performance on FL improves with model size and training steps, consistent with language-model scaling laws. They also claim benchmark performance rises with parameter count for Qwen chat and coder models. They report exceptions: larger models underperform on some tasks, including FL, where stronger models over-flag errors, and an ML example where 14B trails 0.5B.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains models on task-specific formal-language data and measures proof-error prediction performance; it does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy or fit the original loss-scaling or compute-allocation laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Model size and training steps change performance; the paper reports that larger models learn faster early and reach higher performance ceilings in the FL experiment.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of The 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The authors state that computational resources limited assessment of extremely large models and extensive training-data distributions. The scaling curves are presented in Figure 2 without exact values or uncertainty estimates in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Other benchmark scores and model comparisons are not included because they do not report the scaling experiment's trained FL curves or an explicit size-related anomaly bearing on V6.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs extrapolated to larger runs.
No depth/width comparison at fixed parameter count.
Fine-tuning curves are shown, but no power-law form is fitted or tested.
Trends are qualitative only. There is no quantitative predictive fit, and no prediction from pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: Per-size benchmark averages for the Qwen-2.5 (0.5B–72B) and Qwen-2.5-Coder (0.5B–32B) families under each prompting setting
Inverse size trend on the FL subset in the benchmark (smaller models score higher), with the authors' explanation
missing.locator: Sec. 4.2 'stronger models perform worse'; Table 5 FL column

missing.what: Authors' general claim that performance improves with parameter size for Qwen chat and coder models
missing.locator: Sec. 4.2 'Larger model sizes tend to yield better performance'

record.verdict_notes: This is a code-execution benchmark paper; the only scaling evidence is downstream task accuracy. The Figure 2 sweep is task fine-tuning, with values unreadable from text and no uncertainty or fit reported. The Table 5 size trends depend on prompting and subset.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute is not measured.
The study does not fit loss curves on small runs and compare their predictions with larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token compute-optimal split is tested.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study does not test power-law loss scaling across other modalities or training regimes as stated in this version.

The scaling experiment covers formal-language proof-error prediction, not a range of downstream tasks or prediction from pretraining loss; it reports qualitative trends rather than a quantitative predictive fit.
The study does not compare fitting choices, fitted exponents, alternative parameter-counting conventions, or curve bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: Qwen-2.5-14B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared performance with the smaller Qwen-2.5-0.5B-Instruct on ML tasks.
rows.baseline: Qwen-2.5-0.5B-Instruct; exact score not stated in the prose
rows.value: The 14B model was outperformed by the 0.5B model
rows.note: The paper gives this as an example of a larger model performing worse on some complex reasoning tasks.
rows.check: The prose example holds only for zero-shot and some languages. In Table 5 zero-shot ML, 14B is below 0.5B on C++ (9.09 vs 13.64), Rust and Others, but above it on Python, Julia and Java. Under CoT, 14B is far higher (e.g. C++ 68.18 vs 27.27). The condition should say zero-shot; the prompting condition is not 'not stated'.

relationships.condition: FL error-feedback prediction after fine-tuning Qwen 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B, across training steps
relationships.reason: Authors state larger models learn faster and reach higher ceilings (r1-r4). This is qualitative and figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Larger fine-tuned models learned error-feedback prediction faster and reached higher performance ceilings.

relationships.condition: SURGE average score, Qwen-2.5 chat few-shot CoT and Qwen-2.5-Coder series in all three prompting settings (Table 5; text-based, no row)
relationships.reason: Averages rise monotonically with size. Few-shot CoT chat goes 11.17→16.85→21.58→28.71→41.37→43.15→49.99 from 0.5B to 72B.
relationships.display_finding: Average scores increased monotonically with size, including few-shot CoT chat scores of 11.17, 16.85, 21.58, 28.71, 41.37, 43.15, and 49.99 from 0.5B to 72B.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot prompting: Qwen-2.5 chat average and ML subset (Table 5; r5)
relationships.reason: Zero-shot chat averages are non-monotonic: 1.5B 18.80, 7B 15.48, 14B 13.34, 32B 25.08. 14B trails 0.5B on several ML languages (r5). The scale trend depends on prompting.
relationships.display_finding: Average scores were 18.80, 15.48, 13.34 and 25.08 at 1.5B, 7B, 14B and 32B, respectively, with 14B also trailing 0.5B on several ML languages.

relationships.condition: FL subset of the benchmark, zero-shot, Qwen-2.5 chat models (Table 5 and Sec. 4.2; text-based, no row)
relationships.reason: Scores fall with size: 0.5B 42.38, 1.5B 41.72, 14B 7.28, 32B 7.65. Authors attribute this to larger models flagging correct proofs as wrong.
relationships.display_finding: Scores were 42.38 at 0.5B, 41.72 at 1.5B, 7.28 at 14B and 7.65 at 32B, with larger models more often flagging correct proofs as wrong.
